title: Title: SEO vs. GEO: What’s the difference, and does your business need both?
summary: If you run a business, you may have heard a new term alongside SEO: GEO, or generative engine optimization. The distinction is straightforward: SEO helps people find your pages through search results. GEO aims to help your information appear accurately in answers generated by AI systems. They overlap, but they are not interchangeable. What SEO focuses on Search engine optimization helps search engines discover, understand, and rank your content. Typical work includes: Making pages accessible and easy to navigate. Publishing useful content that matches search intent. Improving site speed and mobile usability. Earning relevant links. Using descriptive titles and appropriate structured data. The goal is visibility in search results that can bring qualified visitors to your website. What GEO focuses on Generative engine optimization focuses on how AI answer systems discover, interpret, and potentially cite information about your business. Useful practices include: Answering specific questions clearly. Supporting claims with reliable sources. Keeping business details consistent and current. Explaining who created the content and their relevant experience. Publishing original insights, research, and practical examples. There is no guaranteed formula for getting an AI system to recommend your company. Different systems use different sources, and answers can change with the question, location, and available information. A practical example Imagine someone searches: “Reputation management services for executives.” Traditional search may present a list of pages. SEO helps your relevant page compete for visibility. An AI assistant may instead summarize what to consider when choosing a provider and reference a few sources. GEO work aims to make your expertise understandable and usable in that kind of answer. Being cited does not necessarily mean being recommended—or receiving a website visit. Does GEO replace SEO? No. Many of the foundations support both: accessible pages, useful writing, accurate facts, and credible evidence. AI answer systems may draw on search results, so weakening your SEO foundation to chase GEO can be counterproductive. A sensible starting point is to improve the content you already have: Choose a real customer question. Give a direct answer near the top of the page. Add evidence, examples, and relevant limitations. Make authorship and business information clear. Review the page when facts change. Avoid publishing dozens of repetitive AI-generated pages simply to mention your brand more often. More content does not automatically create more credibility. How should you measure them? For SEO, track relevant rankings, organic traffic, qualified inquiries, and conversions. For GEO, monitor whether your business is mentioned or cited across a consistent set of relevant questions. Check whether those mentions are accurate, and track referral traffic where available. Treat AI visibility measurements as a sample, not a complete picture of what every user sees. The practical takeaway: SEO and GEO both benefit from content that makes your business easier to understand and your claims easier to verify.
